lines.text: On a bad-air morning in Delhi, a teacher with 44 children has one question.
Open the window, or keep it shut?
Keep it shut, and the children's own breath pushes CO₂ past 2,000 ppm in a single period.
The room turns stuffy, and attention drops.
Open it, and almost all of the smog outside comes in.
Khidki, the Hindi word for window, answers that question minute by minute.
It tells the teacher exactly when to open, and when to close.
Children breathe fresher air, the teacher is interrupted less, and the principal sees every classroom on one page.
How does it know when, without extra hardware?
Khidki keeps a physics twin of the classroom: how fast 44 children add CO₂, and how much smog each window setting lets in.
Every morning at six, it takes the outdoor air forecast and the timetable, tests the day in five-minute steps, and keeps the plan with the best balance.
School safety rules are written as Cedar policies, so every decision shows the rule and the number behind it.
During the day, the teacher sees one calm instruction, in Hindi and English.
One tap says it's done.
Khidki never asks more than six times a day.
Did the window really open? There is no sensor on the window.
The children's breath is the tracer gas, so one ordinary CO₂ meter is enough.
How fast the level falls tells Khidki how open the room is.
If only one side opened, it asks for the other.
An AWS Step Functions workflow waits for the tap, waits for the air, and then verifies.
Here is how it is built. Readings come in through API Gateway to Lambda, and live in DynamoDB.
EventBridge starts the 6 AM plan, Step Functions runs every instruction, and Polly speaks it in Hindi.
The whole stack is one CDK app.
Under the hood, the twin and the planner are Python and NumPy: dynamic programming for the plan, a least-squares fit for the window check.
The screens are React and TypeScript.
131 automated tests keep it honest, and everything also runs on a laptop with no cloud.
We tested it on 48 real Delhi school days from last winter, in a simulated classroom.
Against a CO₂ alarm, Khidki cut stuffy minutes from 65 a day to 17, with 4 requests to the teacher instead of 15.
It lets in a little more smog to do that, and we say so plainly.
In this hackathon we built the teacher's screen, the principal's page, and a timetable any school can print with no sensor at all.
It is deployed on AWS, and the code is open.
Khidki. Open the window at the right minute.
